html:
The Malacca Sultanate was a Malay port kingdom on the Strait of Malacca, founded around 1400 and conquered by Portugal in 1511. For a century it was one of the busiest trading ports in the world.

Its founder was Parameswara, a prince from Palembang who claimed descent from the kings of Srivijaya. Driven out of Singapura, he settled at Malacca, a fishing village with a good harbour on the narrowest stretch of the sea route between India and China.

Why it thrived:

  • Chinese protection. Malacca sought the support of the Ming emperors, and the fleets of Zheng He used it as a base. That shielded it from Siam and Majapahit.
  • Monsoon timing. Ships from India, Arabia, China and the spice islands met there while they waited for the winds to turn.
  • Order and low risk. Each trading community had its own harbour master, and the port had a written maritime code.

Its rulers became Muslim early in the 15th century, and Malacca became a centre for spreading Islam through the archipelago. Its court shaped Malay language, literature and custom; the Malay Annals tell its story. Classical Malay became the common language of trade across island Southeast Asia.

In 1511 a Portuguese fleet under Afonso de Albuquerque took the city. The last sultan, Mahmud Shah, fled south, and his heirs founded the Johor and Perak sultanates. Trade then scattered to other Muslim ports such as Aceh, Johor and Demak. The Dutch took Malacca from the Portuguese in 1641.
sum: The Malacca Sultanate was a Malay port kingdom on the Strait of Malacca, founded around 1400 and conquered by Portugal in 1511. For a century it was one of the busiest trading ports in the world.
